Android from the foundation · Puzzle 1 of 6

An app is a Linux process with its own user

Each app gets its own Linux user ID and its own process. The kernel keeps them apart, so one app can't open another's files or read its memory.

The problem

A phone runs dozens of apps from different companies. A banking app must be safe from a game that wants to read its files or its memory. How do you keep them apart without trusting either of them?

See it

The building block

Android is built on Linux, and Linux already knows how to keep users apart. So Android turns each app into its own user: at install time the app gets a unique user ID (UID), and it runs in its own process.

  • Files the app creates belong to its UID; other apps can't open them.
  • Processes can't read each other's memory.
  • The kernel enforces both, so a buggy or hostile app can't switch them off.

The analogy

An apartment block. Each app has its own flat and its own key. Neighbours can't walk in. To ask for something, they go through the building's official channels.

Check yourself

An app wants to read another app's database file directly. Possible?

No. The file belongs to another UID and the kernel refuses. Apps share data only through official channels such as ContentProviders and Intents.

Who enforces the sandbox: the app, or the kernel?

The kernel. That's why an app can't simply turn it off.

Two apps run at the same time. Do they share one process?

No. Each app runs in its own process, with its own memory.

Sources

  • Android Open Source Project: Application sandbox
  • Android Developers: Processes and threads overview

What you now know

Your app is a house with its own key (a UID) and its own walls (a process). To get anything from another app, you go through official doors, never straight in.
